un Tuesday afternoon Mr. IV. T. II kis band, deputy Coroner, held /111 inquest at the Unicorn Inn. IV inwick-st.. Warring..., regarding the Ileuth of an infant named Richard Findley, who died suddenly on Sunday morning. The mother of the deceased, Bridget Findley, wife of Martin Findley, forge laliottrer. at Philip-AL said that the chtlil wna a month old. The deceased was all right cc Saturday night, and Vii,fl,ol and her husband were sober. She gave the child the breast at two o'clock on Sunday morning, and when she , got up snout after sex o'clock. she saw that it was dead. She gave the child !dyad with a little butter on it. - The Deputy Gunner : A child won't live if you give it that. What you should give a child io onlinary milk witli water in it until it is tune. It is no use giving it bread you might as • well give it sand. They have no b.iness to have bread at that age. You did what you t bought best, hut a Child can be killed that way. I have to tell the same to many people. Martin Findley, father of the deceased. then gave evidence. The Deputy- , comiter told the jury that from the mere fact of a Child having been partly fed on bread he could very easily believe that it would be found dead. There , were no indications of it, biting been smothered, • and in his opittion it would have been alive still if it 1.1 been properly fed.- The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was found dead ' in bed.

But the difficulty i$ that France is not at peace because the (haler.] has pnived to be a disturber ; and as to a dictatorship if he was no unscrupulous as to aim at it, he would have no scruple as to offering a denial. Thou there is the point as to the revision of the eon- stitution ; but as to this we have nothing but generalities, whidi are altogether suspicious because they are altogether vague. WADDINGTON, tbv Frtalch Ambassador, to whom a dinner was given, on Sunday, by the French residents in London. Ho said --• ,

This Constitution, in his opinion, combined the elasticity necessary in a country of universal seffrage, and at the same time guaranteed to the institut 10111 of a great conntry like Franco, with a long policy and traditiollB and glory to defend, that stability which was absolutely necessary. For this reason he was a firm defender of the Constitu- tion.

Robert Rigby. who In employed as an over-looker in a mill at West liam, Essex, wan brought before Sri' Warrington magistrates on Monday, on a charge of baring travelled on the London and North- Western Railway, from Preston to Warrington, xi dhow having paid his tare. Ile said that he must have 10$ the ticket, hut the rail- way offieials,by resorting to the Use of the telegraph, found that only one ticket for London had been issued at Preston, nod that it had been colleeed at Rugby. BURNLEY GAZETTE, Febrilary :23rd. HE lot of those who toil from day to day in the bowels of the earth is not a very agreeable one. Apart from the terrible sin of which we are so often reminded by a calamitous explosion, itb all its thrilling scenes, the collier has to pursue his work at times under circumstances of great hardship. Mr. Moses Knowles, of 1w), Oxford Road, Burnley, has had some experience of the trying conditions of labour in some of the deeper coal mines of this country. He relates how he has repeatedly had to work for hours crouched in ten or twelve inches of water and the cold liquid at the same time dropping all over his body from above. Happily such conditions nf utpioyntent are almost unknown in the Burnley district, but Mr. Knowles has had to eno,lanter them in other mining iu consequence. He first commenced with pains in his . •11 gradtudly extended to other parts of the body.* " said Mr. Knowles, "that I was obliged to be covered ts and have a chair , . It was only then that I could feel anything like warmth. My legs got so weak that I had to have the help of a stick to get across the floor. F was terribly troubled with indiges- tio7l, nervous debility, and disease of the liver and kidneys, and had constant attacks of ming) in the st‘imaelt. For many weeks I suffered dreadfully, writhing in agony for hours together, and zot so weak that it was painful to speak, let alone trying to move. Medicine only sepia Al to make me worse, and 1;...0t so that my friends gave me up and the doctor ventured to olfor no hope of 4 CUM. At last I read ono if Warner's pamphlets, soni for a bottle of Warner's SAFE ii7iti Oh how much good it did iii. In a few weeks I Wai: a 144-4. man. ,ippetite tamped, the \veal: lals disappeared, and I: .-111 INtek to lily stork feeling stronger than I had done for years."

On the 3rd June, Cousden, who was employed as a ropierunner on the canal, was gong , to couple some wagons on to an engine which was tn the floe just at the tap of the cutting at Latchford locks. As he was passing the engine on the narrow space between the lino and the canal he appears to have : slipped, falling to the rocky bottom of the cutting which is thirty feet deep at the point.
